After a month reviewing corrosion papers, he quit — and went to a coding bootcamp. That moment stayed with me. Because hard science takes tremendous efforts and patience, progress rarely happens overnight. But when it does, it changes the world. Take Materials Science as an example, I would believe it is, quite literally, everywhere. From quantum materials to polymers, semiconductors, and beyond — Materials Science shapes the world we live in. And yet, its quiet brilliance often goes unseen. Let’s make this a live discussion, instead of chatting with ChatGPT... 👇 To all brilliant experts, please share one material and one application you know well or you are creating — in one sentence. I will gather them, to learn and for fun! A possible format: Application - Material + Core Function (highlight your company if you like). ➔ F-35 Fighter Jet – Radar-absorbent carbon/polymer composites that hide jet from radar (Lockheed Martin) ➔ Solar Cell – Perovskite film converting sunlight into electricity. ➔ Golden Gate Bridge – Zinc-rich primer shielding steel from salty fog. ➔ Sunscreen – Titanium oxide nanoparticles reflecting UV rays. ♻️ Friends, please repost to help gather more inputs and insights! #MaterialsScience #AdvancedMaterials #HardTech #Research P.S. This move is part of their broader restructuring effort to reduce costs, which includes eliminating unnecessary management layers and shifting focus toward core offerings in client and data center solutions. The layoffs affect a variety of roles such as physical design engineers, software architects, and managers, impacting employees involved in CPU and GPU development. Additionally, Intel has decided to exit the automotive chip market, shutting down its Munich-based division and shifting resources away from modular chip development for autonomous vehicles. This strategic shift aligns with their goal to simplify operations and improve execution speed, emphasizing smaller, more impactful teams. These changes come amid concerns over the company's financial health, with stock prices and market capitalization trending downward over the years, despite reported high revenue and profit margins. No equity. For context: A basic 1-bedroom in San Jose runs $3000+/month. That's $36k/year just for rent - nearly 25% of the take-home pay at the TOP of their range. Silicon photonics is one of the most specialized fields in semiconductors right now. This expertise is critical for AI infrastructure, quantum computing, and next-gen data centers. Companies are making billions on this technology. When I pushed back on the compensation, the response was "we have other roles" instead of addressing the fundamental disconnect between Bay Area cost of living and these offers. Here's the real scenario that Insight Global and other staffing companies are actively participating in: Companies post roles with senior requirements at junior salaries, can't fill them domestically, then claim they need H1B workers who have less negotiating power. It's wage suppression dressed up as a "talent shortage." To my fellow engineers: Know your worth. Don't accept insulting offers that don't even cover basic living expenses. To companies: Check the actual housing costs where you're hiring. If you can't pay enough for your employees to live within an hour of the office, either pay realistic salaries or relocate. In your experience, what’s been the biggest factor in achieving first-pass silicon success? 7 1 Comment Daniel Grodensky Semtech • 1K followers Is a Fully Integrated System-on-Chip LiDAR Still Just a Dream? Nine years ago, a passionate team at Intel, including myself, set out on an ambitious mission to create a fully integrated, low-cost, monolithic LiDAR System-on-Chip. The goal was to combine beam steering, laser sources, coherent detection, and digital signal processing into a single silicon platform. A solution that could transform autonomous vehicles, robotics, and smart infrastructure. We began with a 2D MEMS scanning approach, building on our experience from Intel’s indoor iTOF depth camera. But we quickly realized its limitations. For long-range LiDAR, large mirror apertures were needed to collect enough return photons. And MEMS wasn’t truly solid-state. Drop tests and reliability failures exposed its weakness in automotive environments. We turned to optical phased arrays, encouraged by a talk from Louay Eldada, then CEO of Quanergy, who presented a bold vision of a $250 solid-state LiDAR SoC using a 2D OPA scanner. His famous Stanford talk, which we watched on YouTube, sparked new energy in the team. But that dream eventually collapsed. Quanergy, like many others, didn’t succeed in delivering on the full SoC promise. As we pursued the OPA path, we encountered high two-way insertion loss, poor sidelobe suppression, and complex control requirements that made the system fragile and difficult to scale. Ultimately, we stopped pursuing a fully monolithic SoC and shifted to hybrid approaches, as many in the field have done. We also explored III-V hybrid bonding laser technology to bring lasers directly onto the chip. But we faced major issues with linewidth instability, optical power, thermal drift, and extreme sensitivity to back reflections. The lack of viable on-chip isolation in silicon photonics made this path nearly impossible. That challenge still persists, which is why most of the industry now relies on external laser sources (ELS). Still, the dream is not dead. Today’s advances in co-packaged optics, driven by AI and data center demands, allow excellent in-package integration of ELS, fiber array units, and free-space optics. These enable high-performance, scalable solutions without forcing everything onto a single chip. While monolithic integration may be out of reach for long-range LiDAR, it still holds promise for indoor robotics and short-range applications, where scanner loss and coherent range are less critical, and low-cost integration is the priority. To my former colleagues who once shared this dream, thank you for the journey. We may not have reached the destination, but we helped define the map. 41 2 Comments Youssef O. Hassan Qualcomm • 9K followers 🚀 Wireless data at fiber‑optic speeds — on silicon. Excited to share that our recent work at @UC Irvine on ultrafast F‑band wireless transceivers has been featured in UC Irvine News 🎉 [news.uci.edu] 📡 Our team at the @Nanoscale Communication Integrated Circuits Labs (NCIC Labs) has demonstrated a silicon-based wireless transceiver operating up to ~140 GHz, achieving data rates rivaling fiber‑optic links while maintaining strong energy efficiency — a critical requirement for 6G and FutureG systems. The system introduces a novel architecture that rethinks the digital–analog boundary, enabling: Bits‑to‑antenna transmitters Antenna‑to‑bits receivers As described in the article, this technology has been referred to as a “wireless fiber patch cord,” delivering blistering data rates without physical cables, with applications spanning data centers, automated manufacturing, robotics, AI edge computing, and future wireless infrastructure. 🔬 My contribution (as featured in the article): As the lead author of the antenna‑to‑bits receiver, I discussed the key challenge facing extreme‑speed wireless receivers: “Traditional receivers struggle to catch such fast data without using massive, energy‑draining analog‑to‑digital converters. Moore’s law suggests we can just make transistors smaller to go faster, but at these extreme speeds, we hit a physical wall known as the sampling bottleneck. Youssef Hassan” To address this, our receiver introduces hierarchical analog demodulation, a technique that extracts high‑order modulation directly in the analog domain before digitization: The result is a 22‑nm FD‑SOI receiver consuming only ~230 mW at 120 Gb/s, making this class of sub‑THz radios viable even for portable and power‑constrained platforms. This work is reported in two papers published in the @IEEE Journal of Solid‑State Circuits, covering both the bits‑to‑antenna transmitter and antenna‑to‑bits receiver architectures. Huge thanks to Prof. Payam Heydari, our collaborators, and the NCIC Labs team for an incredible journey pushing the boundaries of analog/RF‑digital co‑design. 📰 News coverage: https://lnkd.in/gwp9_RTT 🔁 Onward toward #Wireless #6G #FutureG #SubTHz #Fband #RFIC #AnalogIC #CMOS #SolidStateCircuits #IEEE #HighSpeedLinks #SemiconductorResearch #UCI 33 Mikhael Lerman US Government • 19K followers ⚖️ From Feminist Reform to Balanced Doctrine When California enacted its equal split community property law, it was a historic reaction to the feminism movement of the time. Women, often excluded from the workforce or earning less than men, needed structural protection to ensure fairness upon divorce. But times have changed. Today, many women are high earners — entrepreneurs, executives, innovators. And paradoxically, the very system that once protected them can now act against them. When a woman becomes the higher contributing spouse, the old equal-split rule can turn protective fairness into financial punishment. That’s where the Doctrine of the Highest and Second Highest Power — and its simple SINE Rule (“Spouse Initiates, Non-initiator Elects”) — come in. It adapts fairness to the realities of modern relationships. It restores symmetry — not favoring one gender over the other, but balancing initiative and choice. A doctrine born in California — but ready for all states.
